estimated_study_time.text: Plan to spend about 2 hours and 15 minutes on this chapter, including reading strategy work, summary-writing practice, grammar review, timed practice, and self-checking.

chapter_summary.text: This lesson provides skills practice for the PTE Academic Summarize written text item type. It focuses on reading a passage under timed conditions, identifying main ideas and supporting points, inferring unknown words, writing a summary, synthesizing information, meeting strict length requirements, and proofreading grammar and punctuation.

evidence_spans.quote: This lesson provides skills practice for the PTE Academic item type Summarize written text.

Reading a passage under timed conditions
• Identifying a writer’s purpose, style, tone or attitude
• Comprehending explicit and implicit information

Identifying the topic, theme or main ideas
• Identifying supporting points or examples
• Inferring the meaning of unknown words

Writing a summary 
• Writing under timed conditions
• Taking notes while reading a text
• Synthesizing information
• Writing to meet strict length requirements
Proofread own writing for grammar and punctuation

meaning.text: A PTE Academic item type that requires test takers to summarize a reading of up to 300 words in one sentence, using correct form, grammar, and vocabulary.

evidence_spans.quote:
The Summarize Written Text test item requires test takers to accurately summarize a reading of up to 300 words 
in one sentence, using correct form, grammar and vocabulary.

meaning.text: A written summary is a brief written statement of the main points of a reading or discussion.

evidence_spans.quote: A brief written statement of the main points of a reading or discussion.

meaning.text: A dependent clause contains a verb but does not make sense on its own.

evidence_spans.quote:
a dependent clause is a clause that contains a verb but which does not make sense on its 
own.

explanation.text: For this item type, test takers write one sentence, have 10 minutes, summarize a reading passage of up to 300 words, and are scored on Content, Form, Grammar, and Vocabulary.

evidence_spans.quote:

explanation.text: A good summary gives all main points, accurately represents the topic and content of the reading, and usually omits examples.

evidence_spans.quote:
All main points need

explanation.text: The simple present tense is usually used in a summary because the writer is giving a factual statement of the reading’s main points.

evidence_spans.quote:
The simple present tense because the writer

core_lessons.title: Find the Main Topic Before Writing

explanation.text: Before summarizing a text, first identify the main topic and think about what you already know about it. This helps you predict what follows, identify main ideas, and guess word meanings.

evidence_spans.quote:
whenever they read a text that they need to summarize they should first identify 
the main topic and think about what they already know about it.

using their knowledge 
of a topic helps them to predict what will follow, and to identify main ideas and guess the meaning of 
words.

core_lessons.title: Use Topic Sentences, Key Words, and Signal Words

explanation.text: Main ideas are often found in a paragraph’s topic sentence, usually the first sentence, but short paragraphs require attention to key words or phrases. Signal words can help distinguish main ideas from supporting ideas, opposing ideas, and examples.

evidence_spans.quote:
the main idea can often be found in a paragraph’s topic sentence, which is usually the first sentence 
of a paragraph.
in short paragraphs, readers need to focus on key words or phrases.

A key skill for recognizing the main point in a paragraph is the ability to use signal words to distinguish main ideas from 
supporting ideas, opposing ideas, and examples.

explanation.text: Writing a summary requires more than copying phrases from the reading. Test takers need to use alternative words and phrases for what they have noted without changing the meaning.

evidence_spans.quote:
writing a summary requires more than just copying phrases from the reading. They 
need to be able to use alternative words and phrases for what they have noted, without changing the 
meaning.

core_lessons.title: Use Dependent Clauses to Add Information

explanation.text: In summaries, dependent clauses are often used to add extra meaning or detail to a noun or noun phrase, and they often follow a key noun and a comma and begin with relative pronouns.

evidence_spans.quote:
In a summary, dependent clauses are often used to add extra meaning or detail to a noun or 
noun phrase.

dependent clauses often follow a key noun and a comma (e.g. ‘a dowry, …’) 
and begin with relative pronouns.

example.text: Compare two summaries of the same passage. Summary A says: "The passage was about a test where people read and write." Summary B says: "The Summarize Written Text item requires test takers to summarize a reading of up to 300 words in one sentence using correct form, grammar, and vocabulary." Summary B is stronger because it is more specific, includes key task requirements, and stays formal.

explanation.text: The source identifies Summary 3 as the best because it presents the main points accurately, omits examples, uses vocabulary, spelling, and grammar accurately, uses the simple present tense, and is within the word limit.

evidence_spans.quote:
Summary 3 presents the main points accurately, omits examples, and accurately uses vocabulary, 
spelling and grammar (including the simple present tense). It is also within the word limit for this 
item.

worked_examples.title: Combining Ideas with a Dependent Clause

example.text: Notes: dowries began as gifts from parents; dowries had several functions; dowries are still used in some traditional cultures. One-sentence summary: "A dowry, which began as a family gift and developed several functions, remains part of marriage in some traditional cultures."

explanation.text: The source explains that dependent relative clauses beginning with which, who, or that can add more information to a noun phrase, and that noun phrases can combine information from two or three paraphrased notes.

evidence_spans.quote:
one way of doing this is to use noun phrases that combine information from  
two or three paraphrased notes.

dependent relative clauses (beginning with  
‘which’, ‘who’ or ‘that’) are a good tool for adding more information to a noun phrase.

example.text: Read a short passage about public figures and privacy. Identify the central claim, note the main reasons, and write one sentence that combines them without adding personal opinion.

explanation.text: The sample summary says that media scrutiny of public figures should be supported because politicians need to be monitored for policy concerns and other public figures depend on the general public for their income.

evidence_spans.quote:
Media scrutiny of public figures should be supported because politicians need to be monitored for policy concerns 
and other public figures depend on the general public for their income.

misconception.text: A summary should include the writer’s personal opinions and examples from the passage.

correction.text: A summary should accurately represent the topic and content, include all main points, and usually omit examples.

evidence_spans.quote:
All main points need 
to be given, the topic and content of the reading needs to be accurately represented, but examples 
are usually omitted.

misconception.text: Copying phrases from the reading is enough to write a successful summary.

correction.text: Writing a summary requires more than copying phrases; test takers need to use alternative words and phrases without changing the meaning.

evidence_spans.quote:
writing a summary requires more than just copying phrases from the reading. They 
need to be able to use alternative words and phrases for what they have noted, without changing the 
meaning.

misconception.text: A response can be written in two sentences as long as the content is accurate.

correction.text: The Summarize Written Text item requires one sentence.

evidence_spans.quote:
The Summarize Written Text test item requires test takers to accurately summarize a reading of up to 300 words 
in one sentence

question.text: List four requirements or scoring factors for the Summarize written text item type that you should check before submitting your response.

answer.text: Check that the response is one sentence, completed within 10 minutes, based on a reading of up to 300 words, and written with attention to Content, Form, Grammar, and Vocabulary.

question.text: Rewrite this note pair as one summary sentence using a dependent clause: dowries originated as gifts from parents; dowries are still part of marriage in some traditional cultures.

answer.text: A possible answer is: "A dowry, which originated as a gift from parents, is still part of marriage in some traditional cultures."

question.text: When reading a paragraph for summary writing, what should you look for if the main idea is not obvious from the first sentence?

answer.text: Look for key words or phrases, and use signal words to separate main ideas from supporting ideas, opposing ideas, and examples.

question.text: Give two ways to guess the meaning of an unfamiliar word while reading under test conditions.

answer.text: Use the meaning of related words, identify the word’s grammatical class, or use the root or main part of the word to help guess its meaning.

review_checklist.text: I can state the task requirements: one sentence, 10 minutes, up to 300 words in the reading passage, and scoring for Content, Form, Grammar, and Vocabulary.
I can identify the main points of a passage and leave out unnecessary examples.
I can paraphrase key phrases without changing the meaning.
I can combine two or three notes into one grammatically accurate summary sentence.
I can use dependent clauses to add detail to a noun or noun phrase.
I can leave time to check grammar, punctuation, spelling, sentence count, and word limit.
